arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Malcolm Stewart argued the statute prohibits registering marks that disparage persons or institutions.
The government argued the provision helps further the purpose of trademark protection by preventing disparagement.
Justice Breyer questioned how the disparagement provision relates to the core purpose of identifying product sources.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The Supreme Court examines the constitutionality of a federal law that bars registration of trademarks deemed disparaging.

paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on January 18, 2017.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Simon Tam wants the court to strike down the law that blocked his trademark registration.
The government wants the court to uphold the law that allows it to reject offensive trademarks.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Tam argues the government cannot deny registration based on its own subjective judgment of a mark's meaning.
The government argues the provision serves a valid purpose by preventing the registration of marks that insult others.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kagan asked why the government's refusal to register a mark is not a viewpoint-based distinction.
Justice Kennedy asked whether copyright law constitutes a government program subject to these constraints.
